notes: Classic GoldSrc Half-Life Deathmatch, i.e. the stock 'valve' mod run by the Half-Life Dedicated Server tool (app 90, hlds.exe / hlds_run -game valve). This file is NOT Half-Life Deathmatch: Source (app 360), which speaks the TCP Source RCON protocol instead. GoldSrc RCON is its own thing: connectionless UDP datagrams on the game port (default 27015, set with -port/+port), with a 'challenge rcon' round trip before every command, guarded by the rcon_password cvar - hence flavour 'custom'. There is no enable setting; RCON is live as soon as rcon_password is non-empty. Engine command forms taken from the ReHLDS reimplementation of the original engine: 'usage:  kick < name > | < # userid > [reason]', 'Usage:  banid <minutes> <uniqueid or #userid> { kick }  Use 0 minutes for permanent', 'Usage:  removeid <uniqueid | #slotnumber>'. {duration} for ban is MINUTES and 0 means permanent. The GoldSrc console tokenizer splits ':' into its own token, and Host_Kick_f, SV_BanId_f and SV_RemoveId_f all reassemble a STEAM_x:y:z argument from those pieces - so the id must be passed UNQUOTED. 'kick #STEAM_0:1:12345' works, but 'kick "#STEAM_0:1:12345"' does not, because the quoted form is one token and the reassembly then produces a broken id. If a deployment prefers names, 'kick "<name>"' is the older documented form and matches the player name exactly (case-insensitive). banid only changes the in-memory filter list; run 'writeid' afterwards to persist it, which rewrites banned.cfg (cvar bannedcfgfile, default banned.cfg, in the mod directory) with one 'banid 0.0 <uniqueid>' line per permanent ban - temporary bans are deliberately not written. Likewise removeid needs a following 'writeid' to survive a restart. IP bans are a separate list (addip/removeip/listip, persisted with writeip to listip.cfg) and are not covered by banList here. 'status' is the roster source; over RCON the address column is present because rcon commands execute with console source. Bots and HLTV proxies print BOT or an hltv: field instead of a STEAM_ id and are dropped by linePattern. 'say' broadcasts as '<hostname> message' and the engine truncates the message at 63 characters. Sources agree on all four core operations; the only point where published guides are thinner than the engine is the Steam-ID form of kick, which is confirmed in engine code but usually documented only as name or # userid.
